course.title: Web Development for Beginners: HTML, CSS & JavaScript from Scratch
course.description: Learn to build real websites from scratch using HTML, CSS, and JavaScript with 5 guided projects.
course.longDescription: A complete, step-by-step introduction to modern web development designed for absolute beginners. Learn how the web works, set up VS Code, master HTML5 structure, style beautiful layouts with modern CSS (Flexbox & Grid), and bring websites to life with interactive JavaScript logic — building 5 real-world projects from a personal bio page to a full Todo app with localStorage.

authors.name: Musa Musa Kannike
authors.bio: A fullstack developer specializing in web, cross-platform mobile, and desktop applications

whatYouWillLearn: Set up VS Code, Live Server, and Chrome DevTools like a professional web developer
Build clean, accessible, semantic web pages with HTML5 markup
Style modern layouts with CSS3, the Box Model, Flexbox, and CSS Grid
Make websites fully responsive across mobile phones, tablets, and desktops

exercise.title: Chapter 1 Capstone Assessment: Web Architecture & Tooling
exercise.instructions: Test your grasp of client-server communication, file paths, developer tools, and editor workflows. These questions are designed to challenge your technical reasoning.

questions.question: When a user enters "https://example.com/about.html" in their browser, what is the exact role of the browser in this transaction?
options: It acts as the client: it creates an HTTP request, sends it over the internet to the server, and parses the returned HTML, CSS, and JS to render the visual page
It stores all website files on the user hard drive and generates the webpage offline before connecting
It acts as the server by hosting the database and processing backend transactions directly on the user machine
It compiles HTML into binary machine code and executes it directly on the graphics card
questions.correctAnswer: It acts as the client: it creates an HTTP request, sends it over the internet to the server, and parses the returned HTML, CSS, and JS to render the visual page
questions.explanation: The browser is the client. Its job is to request files from remote servers, receive the raw text files (HTML, CSS, JS), and assemble them visually onto your screen.

questions.question: You edit your HTML file in VS Code and save your changes, but when you look at your browser, the old version of the page is still showing. Which of the following is the most likely root cause?
options: You opened the HTML file as a static file (file:///) instead of using Live Server, so the browser did not automatically reload upon saving
HTML tags automatically expire after 10 minutes and require a paid license to refresh
VS Code disables file updates whenever an internet connection is detected
The browser cannot read HTML files that have more than 5 lines of code
questions.correctAnswer: You opened the HTML file as a static file (file:///) instead of using Live Server, so the browser did not automatically reload upon saving
questions.explanation: Opening a file directly via file:/// loads a static snapshot. You must either manually hit the refresh button in your browser or serve it through an extension like Live Server that triggers automatic reloads.

questions.question: An engineer right-clicks on a headline on a live website, selects "Inspect", and edits the text directly inside Chrome DevTools Elements panel. What actually happens?
options: The text changes only in the local memory of that engineer browser session; the actual server file remains unchanged
The change is immediately pushed to the website server and becomes visible to every visitor worldwide
The browser crashes because DevTools is read-only and forbids live DOM manipulation
The website domain registrar receives an alert and locks the web page for security reasons
questions.correctAnswer: The text changes only in the local memory of that engineer browser session; the actual server file remains unchanged
questions.explanation: DevTools is purely a client-side debugging tool. Any edits you make in the Elements tab only alter your computer local view of the DOM and disappear as soon as the page is reloaded.

questions.question: Why is naming your primary home webpage "index.html" considered a universal standard across web servers?
options: Web servers are configured by default to look for and serve "index.html" as the root directory default landing file when visitors load a domain
HTML parsers fail with a fatal syntax error if the file name is anything other than index.html
Operating systems like Windows and macOS only permit web browsers to open files starting with the letter "i"
Google Search excludes any website whose homepage file is not named index.html
questions.correctAnswer: Web servers are configured by default to look for and serve "index.html" as the root directory default landing file when visitors load a domain
questions.explanation: By web convention and server configuration, when someone visits "mywebsite.com", the web server automatically looks for index.html inside the root folder and delivers it without requiring the user to type "/index.html".

questions.question: Suppose your project folder has a subfolder named "assets". Inside "assets" is a picture named "logo.png". If your HTML file is in the root project folder, what is the correct relative path to load this image?
options: assets/logo.png
../assets/logo.png
logo.png/assets
/root/computer/desktop/assets/logo.png
questions.correctAnswer: assets/logo.png
questions.explanation: Since index.html and the "assets" folder are in the same directory, you simply step into the folder: "assets/logo.png". Using "../" would step one level backwards above your project folder.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between what the browser Console panel displays versus what the Elements panel displays in Chrome DevTools?
options: Elements displays the live HTML tree and active CSS styles, while Console displays JavaScript logs, script errors, and warnings
Elements displays JavaScript memory leaks, while Console displays HTML headings and paragraph tags
Elements allows you to download files, while Console allows you to edit images
There is no difference; both panels show the identical raw server response
questions.correctAnswer: Elements displays the live HTML tree and active CSS styles, while Console displays JavaScript logs, script errors, and warnings
questions.explanation: The Elements panel shows the DOM hierarchy and CSS styling cascade. The Console tab is the command center for running JavaScript, reading console.log statements, and viewing script errors.

questions.question: A beginner programmer writes code in Microsoft Word and saves it as "index.html". Why will this file often fail or look broken when opened in a browser?
options: Word processors insert hidden rich-text formatting, smart quotes, and metadata that corrupt pure plain-text code syntax
Microsoft Word files can only be read on Windows computers, not on the web
Word automatically encrypts all HTML files with a password
Browsers only accept files created by companies that build web browsers
questions.correctAnswer: Word processors insert hidden rich-text formatting, smart quotes, and metadata that corrupt pure plain-text code syntax
questions.explanation: Code editors like VS Code save files as pure plain text without hidden styling or curly quotation marks. Word processors add hidden XML tags and smart styling characters that break code parsers.

questions.question: Consider this scenario: You see an error in the DevTools Console saying "Failed to load resource: net::ERR_FILE_NOT_FOUND (style.css)". What is the diagnosis?
options: The HTML file is referencing a CSS file at a path or file name that does not exist in the designated directory
The CSS file has more than 50 lines of code which exceeds the browser file size limit
The internet router disconnected because CSS files require high-speed fiber internet
The browser needs to be uninstalled and reinstalled
questions.correctAnswer: The HTML file is referencing a CSS file at a path or file name that does not exist in the designated directory
questions.explanation: ERR_FILE_NOT_FOUND means the browser looked where your code instructed it to look, but found nothing. This usually stems from a typo in the file name or a wrong relative folder path.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes why the separation of HTML, CSS, and JavaScript into separate files is considered an industry best practice?
options: It enforces separation of concerns: structure (HTML), visual presentation (CSS), and interactive behavior (JS) can be maintained and updated independently
Browsers refuse to run any HTML file that contains more than 10 lines of CSS inside it
Web servers charge higher hosting fees if all three languages are written inside a single file
Computers overheat when parsing multiple programming languages inside the same text document
questions.correctAnswer: It enforces separation of concerns: structure (HTML), visual presentation (CSS), and interactive behavior (JS) can be maintained and updated independently
questions.explanation: Separation of concerns keeps codebases clean and scalable. You can redesign the look of a 100-page website by modifying one CSS file without touching the underlying HTML markup.

questions.question: What happens under the hood when Live Server runs inside VS Code on your machine?
options: It spins up a local web server (usually at http://127.0.0.1:5500) and injects a small script that refreshes the browser whenever a saved change is detected
It permanently uploads your website to a public web domain accessible to anyone in the world
It compiles your HTML into a desktop executable application (.exe or .app)
It disables your computer firewall and sends all keystrokes to a cloud server
questions.correctAnswer: It spins up a local web server (usually at http://127.0.0.1:5500) and injects a small script that refreshes the browser whenever a saved change is detected
questions.explanation: Live Server runs a lightweight local HTTP server on port 5500. When you press save, it triggers a live websocket signal that tells the connected browser tab to reload immediately.

Why are tags like ,

options: They cannot hold child text or nested elements, so a closing tag like </img> is invalid and unnecessary
They only work when the computer is disconnected from the internet

questions.question: What happens if a developer omits the "alt" attribute completely from an tag on a public website?
options: Screen readers for visually impaired visitors will read out the ugly, raw file name/URL, and search engine image indexers will be penalized
The browser throws a fatal console error and halts rendering of the entire webpage
The image will automatically be rendered in grayscale mode
The browser replaces the missing image with a default stock photo of a cat
questions.correctAnswer: Screen readers for visually impaired visitors will read out the ugly, raw file name/URL, and search engine image indexers will be penalized
questions.explanation: Omitting the alt attribute hurts accessibility. Screen readers announce the raw file path, and if the image fails to load, users have zero context about what was supposed to be there.

questions.question: A developer writes the following anchor tag: Contact Us. When clicking this link, what modern security risk should they mitigate, and how?
options: The newly opened page can access window.opener; they should add rel="noopener noreferrer" for security and privacy protection
The link will download a malware script unless type="secure" is declared on the anchor tag
Target blank forces the computer to restart unless rel="safe" is added
Target blank requires the user to input their password twice before navigating
questions.correctAnswer: The newly opened page can access window.opener; they should add rel="noopener noreferrer" for security and privacy protection
questions.explanation: Opening links in new tabs with target="_blank" historically exposed a vulnerability where the target page could redirect the opener tab. Modern browsers mitigate this, but adding rel="noopener noreferrer" remains the recommended industry practice.

questions.question:
Consider this file tree:
- project/
  - index.html
  - pages/
    - about.html
  - images/
    - banner.jpg

What is the exact relative path needed inside "about.html" to display "banner.jpg"?
options: ../images/banner.jpg
images/banner.jpg
./banner.jpg
../../images/banner.jpg
questions.correctAnswer: ../images/banner.jpg
questions.explanation: Inside "about.html", you are in the "pages/" subfolder. You must first navigate up one level with "../" into "project/", and then enter "images/banner.jpg".

questions.question: Why is it considered a major SEO and accessibility anti-pattern to use an <h1> tag multiple times across different headings on the same single webpage?
options: The <h1> represents the primary topic title of the entire document; multiple <h1>s confuse search crawlers and screen reader document outlines
The browser limits pages to a maximum of 100 total characters inside <h1> tags
Multiple <h1> tags cause the CSS styling engine to crash
Search engines automatically ban any domain that includes more than one <h1> tag
questions.correctAnswer: The <h1> represents the primary topic title of the entire document; multiple <h1>s confuse search crawlers and screen reader document outlines
questions.explanation: A webpage should have exactly one <h1> representing the main page title. Subheadings should follow a logical descending tree structure: <h2>, followed by <h3>, etc.

questions.question: What is the exact difference between <strong> vs <b>, and <em> vs <i> in modern HTML5 semantic specifications?
options: <strong> and <em> convey semantic importance and emphasis (announced with inflection by screen readers), while <b> and <i> are purely visual stylistic overrides
<b> and <i> load faster because they have fewer letters than strong and em
<strong> can only be used on numbers, while <b> can only be used on alphabet letters
There is no difference; they are 100% interchangeable synonyms in every browser specification
questions.correctAnswer: <strong> and <em> convey semantic importance and emphasis (announced with inflection by screen readers), while <b> and <i> are purely visual stylistic overrides
questions.explanation: HTML5 is semantic. <strong> signals high importance or urgency, and <em> implies vocal emphasis. In contrast, <b> and <i> are typographic styles without semantic weight.

questions.question: You want to create an anchor link that, when clicked, smoothly jumps down the page to a specific section titled "Frequently Asked Questions" on the same page. How is this achieved in HTML?
options: Set Jump to FAQ and give the destination section
Set Jump to FAQ and give the section
Set Jump to FAQ and give the section
Set Jump to FAQ and use JavaScript to force scroll
questions.correctAnswer: Set Jump to FAQ and give the destination section
questions.explanation: Internal page bookmark links use the hash "#" symbol matching the unique "id" attribute of the target element: <a href="#my-id"> jumps to id="my-id".

questions.question: Which of the following describes the behavior of whitespace (multiple spaces, tabs, and newlines) inside normal HTML text when rendered by the browser?
options: The browser collapses consecutive whitespace characters into a single space unless the text is wrapped in a <pre> tag or styled with CSS white-space
The browser faithfully renders every single space and tab exactly as typed in the code editor
The browser replaces extra spaces with bullet points
The browser throws an uncaught whitespace parsing exception in the console
questions.correctAnswer: The browser collapses consecutive whitespace characters into a single space unless the text is wrapped in a <pre> tag or styled with CSS white-space
questions.explanation:
HTML whitespace collapsing means 50 spaces or 10 empty lines in your HTML code will only display as a single space in the browser. To force line breaks, you must use tags like

or
.

questions.question: A student includes a video on their website using <video src="movie.mp4"></video>, but visitors report that they cannot start or pause the video. What crucial attribute was omitted?
options: controls — which instructs the browser to render the native play, pause, volume, and timeline interface
playable — which licenses the video codec for web streaming
allow-user — which grants click permissions to visitors
stream="true" — which connects the video file to the graphics buffer
questions.correctAnswer: controls — which instructs the browser to render the native play, pause, volume, and timeline interface
questions.explanation: Without the "controls" attribute, the video will sit frozen as a static frame without play/pause buttons, volume slider, or seek bar unless custom JavaScript controls are implemented.

exercise.title: Chapter 3 Capstone Assessment: Forms, Data Tables & Semantic Architecture
exercise.instructions: Test your mastery of form submission workflows, label associations, input validations, table data structures, and semantic outlines.

questions.question: A developer builds a form with two radio buttons for "Subscription Plan" (Monthly vs Annual), but when a user clicks Monthly and then clicks Annual, BOTH radio buttons remain selected. What syntax mistake was made?
options: The developer gave both radio buttons different "name" attributes instead of sharing the exact same "name"
Radio buttons cannot be used inside forms without a backend SQL database
The developer forgot to put both radio buttons inside an <h1> tag
Radio buttons are deprecated in modern HTML and always multi-select
questions.correctAnswer: The developer gave both radio buttons different "name" attributes instead of sharing the exact same "name"
questions.explanation: Radio buttons belong to a mutually exclusive group only if they share the exact same "name" attribute value. If their name attributes differ, the browser treats them as independent choices.

questions.question: What is the exact technical benefit of linking an <input id="user-email"> to a <label for="user-email"> rather than just typing plain text beside the input box?
options: Clicking on the label text automatically shifts keyboard focus into the input box, and screen readers read the label when the input is selected
It automatically encrypts the entered email with 256-bit AES encryption before submitting
It ensures the email address is verified with Google servers prior to typing
It changes the background color of the input box to green
questions.correctAnswer: Clicking on the label text automatically shifts keyboard focus into the input box, and screen readers read the label when the input is selected
questions.explanation: The "for" attribute on <label> matching the "id" on <input> binds them together. This enlarges the clickable touch target (vital for mobile users) and provides proper assistive labeling for screen readers.

questions.question: When submitting sensitive user data like passwords or credit card information in an HTML form, why must the form method be "POST" rather than the default "GET"?
options: GET appends all form field values directly into the browser address bar as visible URL query parameters, exposing secrets in browser history and server logs
GET forms cannot contain more than 10 total letters of text
POST forms run 500 times faster across cellular connections
GET forms can only be sent to search engines like Bing and Yahoo
questions.correctAnswer: GET appends all form field values directly into the browser address bar as visible URL query parameters, exposing secrets in browser history and server logs
questions.explanation: Method GET encodes data into the URL query string (e.g. login.html?password=123), which is logged in history and visible on screen. Method POST packages data inside the HTTP request body.

questions.question: Consider an HTML table where one header cell needs to span across three columns horizontally (e.g., "Quarterly Revenue" across Jan, Feb, Mar). Which attribute achieves this?
options: <th colspan="3">Quarterly Revenue</th>
<th rowspan="3">Quarterly Revenue</th>
<th span="3">Quarterly Revenue</th>
<th width="3col">Quarterly Revenue</th>
questions.correctAnswer: <th colspan="3">Quarterly Revenue</th>
questions.explanation: The "colspan" attribute tells a table cell to stretch across multiple horizontal columns. "rowspan" stretches downwards across vertical rows.

questions.question: A developer adds <input type="email" required> to a form. What does the browser do when a user clicks the submit button with the input field left blank?
options: The browser halts form submission automatically and displays a localized validation tooltip stating the field must be filled in
The browser sends a null payload to the server and refreshes the page
The browser closes the tab immediately
The form converts the blank field into the word "REQUIRED"
questions.correctAnswer: The browser halts form submission automatically and displays a localized validation tooltip stating the field must be filled in
questions.explanation: HTML5 client-side validation prevents the form from firing its submit action if required fields are empty or if email inputs do not contain an "@" symbol.

questions.question: In semantic HTML5, what is the subtle architectural difference between a <section> element and an <article> element?
options: An <article> is a self-contained piece of content that could stand alone on another site (like a news story), while a <section> groups related thematic content within a larger page
An <article> can only contain text, whereas a <section> can only contain pictures
A <section> is an older HTML4 tag, whereas <article> is only used in mobile apps
There is no difference; browsers treat them as identical aliases for <div>
questions.correctAnswer: An <article> is a self-contained piece of content that could stand alone on another site (like a news story), while a <section> groups related thematic content within a larger page
questions.explanation: Use <article> when the content makes complete sense on its own if republished elsewhere (e.g., a blog post, a review, a product listing). Use <section> to divide a page into thematic chapters.

questions.question: Why should developers write <button type="button"> instead of just <button> inside an HTML form when the button is meant to trigger a JavaScript action (like opening a modal)?
options: The default type for a button inside a form is "submit", so clicking it without type="button" will unintentionally submit the form and reload the page
Buttons without type="button" cannot be clicked on touchscreen devices
Browsers render buttons without a type in red with a warning icon
The button will delete all user inputs if type="button" is omitted
questions.correctAnswer: The default type for a button inside a form is "submit", so clicking it without type="button" will unintentionally submit the form and reload the page
questions.explanation: Inside a form, any <button> defaults to type="submit". If you want a button to trigger helper actions without submitting the form, you must explicitly declare type="button".

questions.question: What is the structural role of the <thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot> elements inside an HTML <table>?
options: They semantically partition header rows, body data rows, and summary footer rows, allowing browsers and print styles to scroll body rows while locking headers
They convert the table data into an interactive 3D pie chart
They compress table cell text to save bandwidth on servers
They prevent users from copying text from the table
questions.correctAnswer: They semantically partition header rows, body data rows, and summary footer rows, allowing browsers and print styles to scroll body rows while locking headers
questions.explanation: Partitioning tables with <thead>, <tbody>, and <tfoot> improves accessibility, aids CSS styling, and allows long printed tables to repeat the header on every printed page.

questions.question: A contact form has a message field that needs to accept multi-line paragraphs from customers. Why is <textarea> used instead of <input type="text">?
options: <input type="text"> is strictly a single-line input field, whereas <textarea> allows multiline text entry with custom rows and columns
<input type="text"> limits users to 5 characters total
<textarea> automatically corrects grammar and spelling in 40 languages
<input type="text"> only accepts numbers and symbols
questions.correctAnswer: <input type="text"> is strictly a single-line input field, whereas <textarea> allows multiline text entry with custom rows and columns
questions.explanation: <input type="text"> ignores the Enter key and only allows a single line of input. For notes, essays, or long messages, <textarea> is the dedicated multiline input element.

exercise.title: Chapter 4 Capstone Assessment: CSS Specificity, Inheritance & Box Model Mechanics
exercise.instructions: Test your understanding of the CSS cascade, specificity weight calculations, box-sizing geometry, relative units, and margin collapsing.

Red — because class selectors always override ID selectors in modern CSS specifications
Green — because the element selector is declared last in the stylesheet
Black — because conflicting styles cancel each other out to the browser default
questions.correctAnswer: Blue — because an ID selector (#featured) has higher specificity (1-0-0) than class (0-1-0) or element (0-0-1) selectors
questions.explanation: The CSS cascade resolves conflicts using specificity hierarchy: Inline styles (1000) > IDs (100) > Classes/Attributes/Pseudo-classes (10) > Elements/Pseudo-elements (1). The ID selector (#featured) wins decisively.

options: 350px (300px width + 40px left/right padding + 10px left/right borders)
300px exactly, because the width is explicitly set to 300px
325px (300px + 20px padding + 5px border)
370px because margins are automatically added by content-box
questions.correctAnswer: 350px (300px width + 40px left/right padding + 10px left/right borders)
questions.explanation: Under the default "content-box" model, padding and borders are added on top of the declared width. Total width = 300 + 20(left) + 20(right) + 5(left) + 5(right) = 350px. Switching to box-sizing: border-box would keep it at 300px.

questions.question: Two vertical paragraph siblings sit stacked one above the other. The top paragraph has "margin-bottom: 30px;". The bottom paragraph has "margin-top: 20px;". What is the actual vertical distance between them?
options: 30px — due to vertical margin collapsing, adjacent block margins collapse into a single margin equal to the larger of the two
50px — because 30px + 20px adds together normally
10px — because the bottom margin subtracts from the top margin
0px — because margins cannot touch without an explicit divider
questions.correctAnswer: 30px — due to vertical margin collapsing, adjacent block margins collapse into a single margin equal to the larger of the two
questions.explanation: In normal flow, adjacent vertical margins between block elements collapse together. Instead of summing (30+20=50), the browser uses whichever single margin is greater (30px).

questions.question: What is the key architectural difference between declaring font sizes with "rem" units versus "em" units?
options: 1rem is always relative to the root <html> element font size (usually 16px), whereas 1em is relative to the font size of its immediate parent element (which can compound unexpectedly)
rem can only be used on mobile devices, while em only works on desktop monitors
em stands for emergency typography and overrides user browser preferences
rem is an absolute pixel measurement, while em is a percentage of the viewport width
questions.correctAnswer: 1rem is always relative to the root <html> element font size (usually 16px), whereas 1em is relative to the font size of its immediate parent element (which can compound unexpectedly)
questions.explanation: rem (Root EM) anchors directly to the root <html> font-size, keeping measurements consistent and accessible. em scales relative to the parent font size, meaning nested ems multiply and compound.

questions.question: Which of the following CSS properties is inherited by child elements by default from their parent container?
options: color and font-family
border and border-radius
margin and padding
background-color and width
questions.correctAnswer: color and font-family
questions.explanation: Typography and text properties (like color, font-family, font-size, line-height) inherit down the DOM tree naturally so you do not have to restyle every paragraph. Box model properties (margins, borders, padding) never inherit.

questions.question: A developer writes the selector ".navbar .nav-item a:hover". What does this selector target?
options: Any anchor <a> tag that is currently being hovered over, as long as it is nested inside an element with class "nav-item" which is inside an element with class "navbar"
Every link on the entire website simultaneously
Only the navigation bar itself when the mouse touches the screen edge
A JavaScript function named hover inside the navbar module
questions.correctAnswer: Any anchor <a> tag that is currently being hovered over, as long as it is nested inside an element with class "nav-item" which is inside an element with class "navbar"
questions.explanation: This is a descendant selector with a pseudo-class. It traverses from the .navbar ancestor down to .nav-item down to the <a> tag, activating only during the :hover state.

questions.question: Why is using "!important" throughout a CSS stylesheet widely considered a bad practice among senior software engineers?
options: It breaks the natural CSS cascade, makes future maintenance a nightmare, and can only be overridden by writing another even more convoluted !important rule
It increases the browser download time by 5 seconds per line
It disables hardware graphics acceleration in modern web browsers
!important was deprecated in CSS3 and causes stylesheets to fail validation
questions.correctAnswer: It breaks the natural CSS cascade, makes future maintenance a nightmare, and can only be overridden by writing another even more convoluted !important rule
questions.explanation: !important bypasses normal specificity. Overusing it creates an escalation battle where developers have to keep chaining !important to fix basic styles.

questions.question: You want an image banner to have a subtle dark overlay so that white headline text placed on top remains easily readable. Which CSS background function is ideal?
options: linear-gradient(rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.6), rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.6)), url("banner.jpg")
filter: dark-mode(100%)
opacity: -0.5
background-blend-mode: delete-light
questions.correctAnswer: linear-gradient(rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.6), rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.6)), url("banner.jpg")
questions.explanation: Layering a semi-transparent linear-gradient with rgba() on top of a background image creates a dark tint that guarantees high text contrast without needing extra HTML markup.

questions.question: What is the exact color represented by the hexadecimal code "#FFFFFF" and "#000000"?
options: #FFFFFF is pure white (maximum Red, Green, Blue) and #000000 is pure black (zero Red, Green, Blue)
#FFFFFF is pure black and #000000 is pure white
#FFFFFF is bright blue and #000000 is bright red
#FFFFFF is transparent and #000000 is opaque gray
questions.correctAnswer: #FFFFFF is pure white (maximum Red, Green, Blue) and #000000 is pure black (zero Red, Green, Blue)
questions.explanation: Hex codes use base-16 notation for Red, Green, and Blue channels. "FF" is 255 (maximum light), giving white. "00" is zero light, giving pure black.

questions.question: To center a fixed-width block element (such as a card with width: 400px) horizontally within its parent container, which classic CSS margin rule is used?
options: margin: 0 auto;
margin: center;
margin: auto 0;
align: center;
questions.correctAnswer: margin: 0 auto;
questions.explanation: Setting "margin: 0 auto;" sets the top/bottom margin to 0 and tells the browser to divide the remaining left and right horizontal space evenly, centering the block perfectly.

questions.question: When a container is set to "display: flex; flex-direction: column;", which CSS property controls the HORIZONTAL alignment of the flex items across the container width?
options: align-items — because changing flex-direction to column rotates the cross-axis to run horizontally
justify-content — because justify-content always controls horizontal alignment regardless of direction
text-align — because flexbox disables alignment properties in column mode
float: center — because flex items become floats when stacked vertically
questions.correctAnswer: align-items — because changing flex-direction to column rotates the cross-axis to run horizontally
questions.explanation: In Flexbox, "justify-content" always governs the MAIN axis, and "align-items" always governs the CROSS axis. When flex-direction becomes "column", the main axis runs vertically, which means the cross axis (align-items) now controls horizontal positioning.

questions.question: A developer writes "position: absolute; top: 0; right: 0;" on a notification badge, expecting it to pin to the top-right corner of its card container. Instead, the badge shoots to the top-right corner of the whole browser window! What is the missing fix?
options: The parent card container must be given "position: relative;" (or any non-static position) to establish a containing block
The badge must be wrapped in a <marquee> tag
The developer must increase the top value to 1000px
Absolute positioning only works inside <table> elements
questions.correctAnswer: The parent card container must be given "position: relative;" (or any non-static position) to establish a containing block
questions.explanation: An absolutely positioned element searches up the DOM tree for the nearest ancestor with a position other than "static". If no ancestor has position: relative/absolute/fixed, it anchors to the initial viewport (the whole window).

questions.question:
What is the exact behavior of the following responsive CSS Grid property:
"grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fit, minmax(250px, 1fr));"?
options: It creates as many columns as will fit into the row where each column is at least 250px wide, automatically expanding them to fill remaining space and wrapping into fewer columns on smaller screens without media queries
It forces exactly 4 fixed columns on every screen regardless of monitor resolution
It scales the image resolution to 250 megapixels
It crashes the CSS compiler because auto-fit cannot be combined with minmax
questions.correctAnswer: It creates as many columns as will fit into the row where each column is at least 250px wide, automatically expanding them to fill remaining space and wrapping into fewer columns on smaller screens without media queries
questions.explanation: This is the holy grail of responsive grid design. "auto-fit" automatically calculates column count, "minmax(250px, 1fr)" guarantees items are never narrower than 250px, and expands them proportionally to fill row voids.

questions.question: An engineer sets "z-index: 99999;" on a popup modal, yet a dropdown menu with "z-index: 2;" in another header section still appears ON TOP of the modal. What CSS stacking context rule explains this phenomenon?
options: The modal parent container has a lower stacking context (or lower z-index) than the header container; children cannot escape their parent stacking context
z-index values greater than 1000 roll over back to zero like an odometer
z-index only applies to images, not modals or divs
Browsers randomly choose which element renders on top when numbers are uneven
questions.correctAnswer: The modal parent container has a lower stacking context (or lower z-index) than the header container; children cannot escape their parent stacking context
questions.explanation: z-index values are evaluated only within their local stacking context. If Parent A has z-index: 1 and Parent B has z-index: 2, no child inside Parent A (even with z-index: 999999) can ever render above Parent B or its children.

questions.question: Inside a flex container with width 600px, Item A has "flex: 1;", Item B has "flex: 2;", and Item C has "flex: 1;". Assuming no margins or minimum widths, how much width does Item B receive?
options: 300px (2 shares out of 4 total shares: 2/4 of 600px)
200px
400px
150px
questions.correctAnswer: 300px (2 shares out of 4 total shares: 2/4 of 600px)
questions.explanation: The flex shorthand distributes available space proportionally. Total units = 1 + 2 + 1 = 4 units. Each unit = 600px / 4 = 150px. Item B receives 2 units = 150px * 2 = 300px.

questions.question: Why is adopting a "Mobile-First" media query strategy (using min-width) widely preferred in modern production over Desktop-First (using max-width)?
options: Mobile devices have fewer computing resources, so loading simple base styles first and progressively adding complex desktop rules via min-width is faster and cleaner
Google Chrome will refuse to index any site written with max-width queries
max-width queries do not work on Apple iOS devices
Desktop-first code produces larger file sizes that cost more money to host
questions.correctAnswer: Mobile devices have fewer computing resources, so loading simple base styles first and progressively adding complex desktop rules via min-width is faster and cleaner
questions.explanation: Mobile-first design defines lightweight, single-column default styles for mobile, and then layers on advanced desktop layout rules (@media (min-width: 768px)) as screen real estate expands.

questions.question: What is the primary architectural difference between when you should select CSS Flexbox versus CSS Grid?
options: Flexbox is optimized for 1-dimensional layouts (either a row OR a column), whereas CSS Grid is designed for 2-dimensional layouts (rows AND columns simultaneously)
Flexbox is for text only, while CSS Grid is exclusively for photos
Flexbox was designed for mobile apps, while Grid is for desktop monitors
Grid is deprecated and replaced entirely by Flexbox
questions.correctAnswer: Flexbox is optimized for 1-dimensional layouts (either a row OR a column), whereas CSS Grid is designed for 2-dimensional layouts (rows AND columns simultaneously)
questions.explanation: Use Flexbox when you want to arrange items in a single direction (like navigation items in a row, or a centered card). Use Grid when aligning items in a coordinate matrix of both columns and rows.

questions.question: If you want a navigation header to stay visible at the top of the browser window as the user scrolls down through a 5,000-pixel article, which position property should you declare on the header?
options: position: fixed; top: 0; width: 100%;
position: static; top: 0;
position: relative; scroll: lock;
position: absolute; overflow: visible;
questions.correctAnswer: position: fixed; top: 0; width: 100%;
questions.explanation: "position: fixed;" locks the element relative to the browser viewport window so that it never moves during page scrolling. Alternatively, "position: sticky; top: 0;" can be used inside a scrollable container.

questions.question: What does the CSS property "gap: 24px;" accomplish inside a Flexbox or Grid container that older margin workarounds struggled with?
options: It automatically places 24px of space ONLY between child items without adding unwanted outer margins on the first and last edges
It increases the font size of every paragraph by 24 pixels
It forces the browser to wait 24 milliseconds before rendering
It adds a 24-pixel black line between columns
questions.correctAnswer: It automatically places 24px of space ONLY between child items without adding unwanted outer margins on the first and last edges
questions.explanation: The "gap" property cleanly handles gutters between grid cells and flex items without requiring tricky :first-child or :last-child negative margin resets.

options: Any screen with a width of 768 pixels or smaller (such as smartphones and small tablets in portrait orientation)
Only large 4K television monitors
Every device whose screen is wider than 768 pixels
Only Apple computers with Retina screens
questions.correctAnswer: Any screen with a width of 768 pixels or smaller (such as smartphones and small tablets in portrait orientation)
questions.explanation: "max-width: 768px" sets an upper boundary: the rules inside apply to screens up to and including 768px wide.

true, then false

questions.question: What is returned if you run: typeof null in the browser developer console, and why?
options: "object" — this is a famous historical bug from the earliest 1995 implementation of JavaScript that was kept for backwards compatibility
"null" — because null is its own standalone primitive type
"undefined" — because null and undefined are identical synonyms
"boolean" — because null evaluates to false in boolean contexts

options: No — because the "return" statement immediately terminates function execution and hands the value back to the caller
Yes — because console.log always runs before any return statement in JavaScript
Yes — but only if price is an even number
No — because functions cannot return numbers with decimal points

The computer crashes with an OutOfMemory error
It loops infinitely because items.length changes automatically
It prints items[0] again from the beginning

questions.question:
If an object is declared as: const user = { name: "Sarah", age: 24 };
Why does user.age = 25 work without throwing an error, even though "user" was declared with "const"?
options: "const" protects the variable reference binding, not the internal properties of the object; the object itself remains mutable
JavaScript ignores const when operating inside Chrome
Numbers are exempt from the const declaration rules
Because 25 is greater than 24
questions.correctAnswer: "const" protects the variable reference binding, not the internal properties of the object; the object itself remains mutable

null — because mixed logical operators evaluate to null
undefined

options: .map() returns a brand new transformed array containing the return values of each iteration, whereas .forEach() simply executes a function on each element and returns undefined
.map() can only be used on strings, whereas .forEach() is for numbers
.forEach() creates a copy of the array, while .map() deletes the original array
There is no difference; they are exact aliases

options: "Hello friend" — because default parameter values are used whenever an argument is omitted or passed as undefined
"Hello undefined"
"Hello NaN"
A SyntaxError exception

questions.question: Why is using "element.textContent = userInput;" vastly superior to "element.innerHTML = userInput;" when displaying text entered by untrusted users?
options: innerHTML parses and executes any embedded <script> tags or malicious event handlers inside the input, opening a catastrophic Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability, whereas textContent treats all inputs as safe plain text
textContent runs 1,000 times faster on modern CPU cores
innerHTML can only be used on tables, not paragraphs or headings
textContent automatically translates vulgar words into polite synonyms
questions.correctAnswer: innerHTML parses and executes any embedded <script> tags or malicious event handlers inside the input, opening a catastrophic Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) vulnerability, whereas textContent treats all inputs as safe plain text
questions.explanation: Injecting raw user input directly into innerHTML is the #1 vector for Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) attacks. textContent safely escapes HTML characters (< and >) and prints raw text without browser parsing.

questions.question: You have a dynamically generated todo list that might hold 500 items. Instead of attaching 500 individual click event listeners to every single <li>, what professional design pattern should you employ?
options: Event Delegation — attach one single click listener to the parent <ul> container and inspect event.target to see which child item was clicked via event bubbling
Create a while loop that re-attaches 500 event listeners every second
Force the user to reload the page after clicking every task
Store all 500 event listeners in a separate CSS file
questions.correctAnswer: Event Delegation — attach one single click listener to the parent <ul> container and inspect event.target to see which child item was clicked via event bubbling
questions.explanation: Event Delegation relies on event bubbling (events bubble upwards through ancestor nodes). Placing a single listener on the parent improves performance, saves memory, and automatically handles future dynamic children.

questions.question: What happens if a developer runs: localStorage.setItem("userData", { score: 100, level: 5 }); and later retrieves it with localStorage.getItem("userData")?
options: It returns the useless string "[object Object]" because localStorage only stores strings and automatically converts objects using default string coercion
It returns the exact original JavaScript object { score: 100, level: 5 } intact
It throws an unhandled QuotaExceededError in the console
It deletes all other keys stored inside localStorage

questions.question: In an event listener callback, what is the exact technical difference between "event.target" and "event.currentTarget"?
options: event.target is the actual innermost element that was clicked, while event.currentTarget is the element to which the event listener was originally attached
event.target is for keyboard presses, while event.currentTarget is for mouse clicks
event.currentTarget is the browser window, while event.target is the computer mouse
There is no difference; they are interchangeable aliases

questions.question: Why is calling "event.preventDefault()" essential inside a form "submit" event listener in single-page JavaScript applications?
options: It stops the browser from executing its default action of refreshing the page and attempting an HTTP navigation to the form action URL
It clears all user passwords from computer RAM
It forces the form to animate with a sliding transition
It tells the browser to print the form to a PDF document

questions.question: Which method should you use to toggle a CSS class named "dark-theme" on the document <body> so that it is added if missing, and removed if already present?

document.body.style.dark = true;

questions.question: What is the return value of "document.querySelector('.non-existent-class')" when no matching elements are found in the DOM?
options: null
undefined
An empty array []
A fatal DOMException error

questions.question: Consider a situation where you repeatedly rebuild a 100-item list by setting "container.innerHTML = htmlString" inside a loop. Why is this considered an anti-pattern compared to building elements with document.createElement() or DocumentFragment?
options: Repeatedly rewriting innerHTML destroys all existing DOM nodes, removes active event listeners, and forces the browser to re-parse the HTML and recalculate layout on every iteration
innerHTML can only hold up to 10 total characters in Chrome
DocumentFragment requires a monthly paid developer subscription
createElement is deprecated in modern ECMAScript specifications

questions.explanation: Re-assigning innerHTML causes total destruction and re-parsing of the subtree, dropping event listeners and causing layout thrashing. Creating nodes in memory or batching updates with fragments is far more performant.

questions.question: What is the standard storage capacity limit of browser localStorage per origin, and what happens when you exceed it?
options: Approximately 5MB of text data; attempting to store more throws a DOMException: QuotaExceededError
Unlimited gigabytes backed by cloud storage
Exactly 100 kilobytes; exceeding it silently deletes old files
50 megabytes per webpage tab

questions.explanation: localStorage typically provides ~5MB of storage per domain. When full, calling setItem() throws a QuotaExceededError that must be handled with a try/catch block in robust applications.

questions.question: What does the DOM method "element.closest('.card')" do when executed on an element?
options: It traverses upwards through the element and its ancestors in the DOM tree until it finds the closest element matching the selector ".card"
It finds the closest element physically on the screen based on pixel coordinates
It searches downward into child elements only
It closes and deletes the card component
questions.correctAnswer: It traverses upwards through the element and its ancestors in the DOM tree until it finds the closest element matching the selector ".card"
questions.explanation: element.closest(selector) is an invaluable method for event delegation: it walks up the ancestor chain and returns the nearest parent node matching the selector, or null if none match.

topics.title: How the Web Actually Works
topics.description: Discover what happens when you visit a website, and meet the three core languages of the web.

blocks.content:
Welcome to the Web!

Every day, you visit websites on your phone and laptop. You tap links, watch videos, and send messages. But have you ever stopped to wonder: what actually happens when you type a website address like "google.com" and press enter?

It feels like magic, but it is actually a very simple conversation between two computers. Let us see how it works step by step.

Clients and Servers (The Restaurant Analogy)

Imagine you walk into a restaurant and sit at a table:

1. You are the customer. In web terms, your computer or phone is called the **Client**.

2. The kitchen has all the food and cooks the meals. In web terms, the computer that stores the website files is called the **Server**.

3. The waiter takes your order to the kitchen and brings your food back to your table. That delivery system is called the **Internet**.

When you type a web address, your browser (the client) asks the server: "Please send me the home page files." The server finds the files and sends them back to your screen.
Remember: The client is the computer asking for a website; the server is the computer that stores and sends the files.

quiz.question: When you open your phone browser and go to a website, what role does your phone play?

options.text: The Client — because it requests and displays the website files
The Server — because it hosts files for millions of other people
The Database — because it stores all the world web code

quiz.explanation: Remember: The client is the device asking for files; the server is the computer storing and sending them.

blocks.content:
What is a Web Browser?

A web browser is a program on your computer or phone that knows how to read website files. Popular browsers include Google Chrome, Apple Safari, Microsoft Edge, and Mozilla Firefox.

When a server sends raw website files to your computer, they are just plain text files. Your browser reads those text files and paints them into pretty buttons, pictures, and text on your screen.

Without a browser, a website would just look like long pages of code text.

The Three Core Languages of the Web

Every website you have ever visited is built using three languages working together as a team:

1. **HTML (The Skeleton / Bricks):** HTML puts content on the page. It adds headings, paragraphs, buttons, and images.

2. **CSS (The Paint / Clothes):** CSS makes the page look beautiful. It adds colors, spacing, borders, fonts, and sets the layout.

3. **JavaScript (The Brain / Muscles):** JavaScript makes the page do things. When you click a button and a popup opens, or when a timer counts down, that is JavaScript in action.

Think of a house: HTML is the concrete foundation and brick walls. CSS is the paint, tiles, and curtains. JavaScript is the electricity, light switches, and running water.
Remember: HTML provides the structure, CSS provides the style, and JavaScript provides the interactivity.

quiz.question: If you want to change the background color of a website from white to dark blue, which language should you use?

options.text: CSS — because CSS controls colors, beauty, and visual styling
HTML — because HTML is the only language that handles colors
JavaScript — because colors require complex mathematical calculations

quiz.explanation: Remember: HTML builds the structure, CSS adds colors and beauty, and JavaScript handles actions.

topics.title: Anatomy of an HTML Tag & Document Structure
topics.description: Learn how HTML tags work, how attributes add superpowers, and master the standard document template.

blocks.content:
What is an HTML Tag?

HTML stands for **HyperText Markup Language**. You can think of HTML as wrapping everyday text with special label tags so the computer knows what each piece of text is supposed to be.

Imagine you have a moving box. If you write "Kitchen Dishes" on the box, movers know to treat it carefully. HTML tags are those labels for the browser.

The 3 Parts of an HTML Element Most HTML elements are made of three simple parts: 1. **Opening Tag:** `

` (tells the browser: "a paragraph starts here") 2. **Content:** `Hello World` (the actual text or picture inside) 3. **Closing Tag:** `

` (tells the browser: "this paragraph ends here") Notice the forward slash `/` in `

`. That slash is how the browser knows the tag is finished. If you forget the closing tag, the browser gets confused about where your element ends! Remember: An HTML element has an opening tag ``, content in the middle, and a closing tag `` with a slash.

options.text: By using a closing tag with a forward slash, like
By typing the word END in all capitals

quiz.explanation:
Remember: Closing tags always have a forward slash right after the left angle bracket (for example,

).

blocks.content:
What are Tag Attributes? Attributes give extra information or superpowers to your tags. They are always written INSIDE the opening tag. An attribute looks like this: `name="value"` For example: `

Welcome!

` Here, `class` and `id` are attributes. They give names to the paragraph so we can color it with CSS or make it move with JavaScript later.

The Starter Boilerplate (The Standard Foundation)

Every professional HTML document has the exact same starter skeleton:

1. `<!DOCTYPE html>`: Tells the browser: "Hey, this is modern HTML5!"
2. `<html lang="en">`: The root container holding everything on the page.
3. `<head>`: Contains behind-the-scenes settings (page title, fonts, links to CSS). Visitors do not see this content on the page.
4. `<body>`: Contains everything visitors actually see and touch (text, buttons, pictures).

Remember: All visible website content belongs inside the <body> tag; behind-the-scenes settings belong inside <head>.

quiz.question: Where do you put the headings, images, and text that you want visitors to see on your website?
quiz.explanation: Remember: Everything visible to users goes inside <body>. The <head> is only for behind-the-scenes settings.

topics.title: The DOM Explained: Selecting Elements
topics.description: Understand how JavaScript views your HTML as a living tree, and grab elements with querySelector.

blocks.content:
What is the DOM?

DOM stands for **Document Object Model**. When the browser opens your `index.html` file, it does not just stare at text. It turns every tag into a living JavaScript object and organizes them into a family tree.

The `<html>` tag is the trunk of the tree. The `<head>` and `<body>` are main branches. Headings, buttons, and paragraphs are smaller branches and leaves.

Selecting Elements from JavaScript

Before you can change an element, your JavaScript code needs to "grab" it. The most modern, versatile way is **`document.querySelector()`**.

You pass it the exact same selector you use in CSS:
- By ID: `document.querySelector("#my-button")`
- By Class: `document.querySelector(".card-title")`
- By Tag: `document.querySelector("h1")`

If you want to grab ALL matching elements (like all 10 buttons on a page), use **`document.querySelectorAll(".btn")`**.
Remember: The DOM is the living tree of HTML elements; document.querySelector() selects elements using standard CSS selectors.

quiz.question: How do you grab an HTML button with id="save-btn" in JavaScript?
quiz.explanation: Remember: document.querySelector("#save-btn") grabs the element matching the CSS ID selector.

topics.title: What is JavaScript & Where Does It Run?
topics.description: Meet the programming engine of the web, connect a script to HTML, and use console.log.

blocks.content:
Welcome to Real Programming!

Up until now, you have learned HTML to create the skeleton of a website and CSS to paint it with colors and layouts. But your webpage is still frozen in time — it cannot think, calculate, or respond to users.

**JavaScript** is the programming language that gives your website a brain. It lets your site calculate math, validate forms, open menus, save user choices, and load live data from the internet.

Where Does JavaScript Run?

Here is something amazing: You do not need to install any complex software to run JavaScript. Every web browser on earth (Chrome, Safari, Edge) already has a powerful JavaScript engine built right inside it!

To link JavaScript to your HTML, you add a `<script>` tag right before the closing `</body>` tag:

`<script src="script.js"></script>`

Placing it at the bottom of the `<body>` ensures the browser finishes loading all your HTML elements before the JavaScript starts running.
Remember: JavaScript adds logic and brains to your website; link it using <script src="script.js"></script> at the bottom of <body>.

quiz.question: Where should you place the <script src="script.js"></script> tag in your HTML document?

options.text: At the very bottom of the <body> tag, just before </body>
Outside the <html> tag in the trash

quiz.explanation: Remember: Placing <script> right before </body> ensures all HTML elements are loaded before your code runs.

blocks.content:
Your First Line of Code: console.log()

In JavaScript, whenever you want to inspect a value or print a test message, you use `console.log()`.

Think of `console.log()` as a walkie-talkie between your code and you. Whatever message you put inside the brackets gets printed to the Developer Console in Chrome.

Try It Yourself Task:
1. In your project folder, create a new file named `script.js`.
2. In `index.html`, add `<script src="script.js"></script>` right before `</body>`.
3. Type `console.log("I am a JavaScript developer!");` in `script.js` and save.
4. Open your page in Chrome, right-click $\rightarrow$ **Inspect**, click the **Console** tab, and see your message printed in clean text!
Remember: console.log() is your primary tool for testing values and seeing messages in the browser console.

quiz.question: What does console.log("Success"); do in JavaScript?

options.text: It prints the word "Success" into the browser developer console

The Problem with Old Layouts

For years, getting items to sit side-by-side neatly in a row (like navigation links or product cards) was tricky. Developers had to use hacks like `float` or `inline-block`.

blocks.content:
What is a Variable?

Imagine you are packing boxes for a move. You put kitchen mugs in a cardboard box and stick a label on the front that says "Mugs". Whenever you need a mug, you look for that labeled box.

In programming, a **variable** is simply a labeled storage box that holds a piece of information in the computer memory so you can use it again and again.

const vs. let (The Two Keywords You Must Know)

In modern JavaScript, there are two keywords used to create variables:

1. **`const` (Constant):** Use this when the value will NEVER change (like your birth year or website name). Always default to `const`!

2. **`let`:** Use this when the value CAN change later (like a game score, a counter, or a shopping cart total).

Never use the old keyword `var`. It is an outdated way from 1995 that causes strange bugs in modern code.
Remember: Use const for values that stay constant; use let for values that change. Avoid var.

blocks.content:
The Core Data Types in JavaScript

Every piece of information in JavaScript has a type:

1. **String (Text):** Wrapped in quotes: `"Sarah"` or `'Hello World'`.
2. **Number:** Numbers without quotes: `25`, `3.14`, `-10`. (Numbers can do math!).
3. **Boolean:** Exactly two values: `true` or `false`. (Like a light switch that is either ON or OFF).
4. **Undefined:** A variable that was created but never given a value.
5. **Null:** Intentionally empty ("nothing here on purpose").

const userName = "Ada Lovelace"; // String
const userAge = 28;              // Number
let isLoggedIn = true;           // Boolean

console.log(userName + " is " + userAge + " years old.");

Notice how quotes are used for text strings, but numbers have NO quotes. If you put quotes around a number (`"28"`), JavaScript treats it like plain text words instead of a math number!
Remember: Strings are text in quotes; numbers have no quotes; booleans are either true or false.

To align items along the Main Axis (left, center, right), use: **`justify-content`**.
To align items along the Cross Axis (top, center, bottom), use: **`align-items`**.

Spacing Items Evenly with `gap`

Instead of calculating margins on every item, Flexbox lets you add clean space between items with the **`gap`** property:

`gap: 20px;`

This puts 20px between each child without adding annoying extra space to the outer edges.
Remember: justify-content aligns along the main axis; align-items aligns across; gap sets spacing between items.

- The input has `id="user-email"`

Because they match, when a user taps the text "Email Address", the cursor jumps right into the input box! This is a massive help on small smartphone screens.
Remember: Match the label "for" attribute to the input "id" attribute for friendly usability and accessibility.

Every single element on a webpage is a rectangular box. Even round buttons or single words are wrapped in rectangular boxes by the browser.

2. **Padding:** The breathing room INSIDE the box, between the text and the border.

Comparison Operators (How to Compare Values):

- `!==`: Not equal to.
- `>`: Greater than.
- `<`: Less than.
- `>=`: Greater than or equal to.

blocks.content: The Anchor Tag: The Glue of the Web The entire World Wide Web is built on links. In HTML, a link is created with the `` tag (short for "Anchor"). If you just write `Click here`, nothing happens. You need to tell the anchor tag WHERE to take the user. You do that with the `href` attribute (Hypertext REFerence): `Visit Google` The text between `` and `` is the clickable blue text your user sees.

Absolute vs. Relative Links

There are two types of links you will use:

1. **Absolute Link:** Links to an outside website. It always includes the full web address with `https://` (e.g., `https://wikipedia.org`).

2. **Relative Link:** Links to another file inside your own project folder (e.g., `about.html` or `contact.html`). You do not need `https://` because the file is right there in your folder!
Remember: Use absolute links (with https://) for outside websites, and relative links for your own project pages.

Jump Links (Bookmarks on the Same Page)

Flexbox vs. CSS Grid: When to Use Which?

- **Flexbox (1-Dimensional):** Perfect when you want items in a single direction (a single row of buttons or a single column of links).
- **CSS Grid (2-Dimensional):** Perfect when you want both rows AND columns at the same time (like a dashboard, a photo gallery, or an online store product grid).

To turn on Grid, write on the container: `display: grid;`.

The Magic "fr" (Fraction) Unit

In CSS Grid, `1fr` means "1 fraction of the available space".

If you write `grid-template-columns: 1fr 2fr 1fr;`, the middle column will automatically be twice as wide as the two side columns!
Remember: Use Flexbox for 1D rows or columns; use CSS Grid for 2D rows and columns simultaneously.

topics.title: Semantic HTML5 Tags & Best Practices

blocks.content:
What does "Semantic" Mean?

"Semantic" simply means **meaningful**. In old websites, developers used generic `<div>` (division) boxes for everything. Looking at a page full of 200 `<div>` tags made it impossible to tell what was a navigation menu, what was an article, and what was a footer.

HTML5 introduced meaningful tags that describe their purpose to both humans and search engines.

The Core Semantic Tags:

1. `<header>`: The top bar of a website or article (holds logos and welcome titles).
2. `<nav>`: The main navigation menu containing links.
3. `<main>`: The primary, unique content of that specific page (used only once per page).
4. `<section>`: A themed group of content (e.g. "About", "Services", "Pricing").
5. `<article>`: A self-contained item (like a blog post, product card, or review).
6. `<footer>`: The bottom bar (copyright, legal links, contact info).

blocks.content: Adding Pictures with Websites without pictures would be very boring! In HTML, we add pictures using the `` tag. The `` tag is a **self-closing void tag** (it has no ``). Why the "alt" Attribute is So Important Never skip the `alt` attribute! It serves two huge purposes: - **Accessibility:** If a visually impaired person visits your website, their screen-reading tool reads the `alt` text out loud so they know what the picture shows. - **Broken Images:** If your image fails to load (e.g., poor internet connection or wrong file name), the browser prints your `alt` text in its place so the user still understands what was there. CSS Positioning Explained Simply

The `position` property changes how an element is placed on the screen:

1. `static` (Default): Normal flow of the document.
2. `relative`: Positioned normally, but lets you nudge it slightly with `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`.
3. `absolute`: Pulled out of the page flow and placed at exact coordinates relative to its nearest positioned parent container.
4. `fixed`: Pinned directly to the browser window (stays on screen even when you scroll!). Perfect for sticky navigation bars.

topics.title: Reusable Code with Functions

blocks.content:
What is a Function?

Imagine you have a smoothie blender. You do not build a brand new motor every time you want a drink. You build the blender once, and whenever you are thirsty, you drop in fruit (inputs), press the blend button, and pour out a delicious smoothie (output).

In programming, a **Function** is a reusable machine. You write a block of instructions once, give it a name, and then run it whenever you want with different inputs!

Parameters vs. Return Values

- **Parameters (Inputs):** The variable names inside the brackets (`name`). They act as placeholders for whatever data the user passes in.
- **`return` (Output):** Hands the final calculated result back to whoever called the function.

Modern Arrow Functions (`() => {}`):
Modern JavaScript developers also write functions using the arrow syntax:
`const addNumbers = (a, b) => a + b;`
Remember: Functions package reusable instructions; parameters are inputs; return delivers the finished output.

topics.title: Responsive Design with Media Queries
topics.description: Make your website adapt automatically to smartphones, tablets, and desktop computers.

blocks.content:
Why Responsive Design Matters

Over 60% of all web traffic happens on mobile phones! If your website only looks good on a wide laptop screen, mobile visitors will get frustrated and leave.

**Responsive Web Design** means your site automatically bends, stacks, and reshapes itself to look fantastic on any screen size.

Step 1: The Viewport Meta Tag

Always make sure your HTML `<head>` includes this line:
`<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0">`

This tells mobile phones: "Do not shrink this page down like a desktop site; match the real screen width of the phone!"

What is a Media Query?

A media query is an `@media` rule that tells the browser: "If the screen size meets this condition, apply these special styles!"

In the example above, on laptops the cards sit in 3 columns. On screens smaller than 768px (like phones), they stack comfortably in 1 vertical column.
Remember: Media queries with max-width allow your design to rearrange and stack on smaller phone screens.

quiz.question: What CSS rule allows you to apply styles only on screens that are 768px wide or smaller?
quiz.explanation: Remember: @media (max-width: 768px) triggers styles on screens 768px and below.

blocks.content:
What is an Array?

If a variable is a single storage box, an **Array** is a multi-compartment organizer (like an egg carton or shopping list). It lets you store multiple items in one single variable.

Arrays are wrapped in square brackets `[ ]` with commas between items:
`const fruits = ["Apple", "Banana", "Cherry"];`

quiz.explanation: Remember: The first item in a JavaScript array is always at position [0].

topics.title: Browser Memory: Saving Data with localStorage
topics.description: Make data survive page refreshes using localStorage, JSON.stringify, and JSON.parse.

blocks.content:
Why Do Webpages Forget Everything on Refresh?

Have you noticed that whenever you refresh a page, any JavaScript variables (`let count = 5;`) reset right back to zero? That is because regular variables live in the computer temporary RAM.

To save data permanently inside the user browser, we use **`localStorage`**. Data saved in `localStorage` stays there even if the user closes their laptop or restarts their phone!

quiz.question: Why must you use JSON.stringify() when saving an array into localStorage?

options.text: Because localStorage can only store plain text strings, not raw arrays or objects
Because JSON speeds up your internet connection
Because arrays are illegal in browsers

quiz.explanation: Remember: localStorage only accepts string values; JSON.stringify() serializes arrays into text.

Start the line with two slashes (//)
Surround the text in <!-- comment -->
Start the line with an exclamation mark (!)

Indentation speeds up computer CPU clock speeds
Indentation is only required on Linux computers
Indentation is optional in modern Python 3

A 3D virtual reality simulator for games

A Python-specific text editor
A file compression format like .zip
A tool for testing computer monitors

questions.explanation: Python ranges are exclusive of the stop parameter: range(start, stop) starts at start and stops at stop - 1.

questions.question: What does the break statement do when executed inside a loop?
options: Immediately terminates the loop and jumps to the first line of code following the loop
Skips only the current iteration and moves to the next item
Restarts the computer
Pauses execution for 5 seconds
questions.correctAnswer: Immediately terminates the loop and jumps to the first line of code following the loop
questions.explanation: break immediately exits the enclosing loop entirely, ignoring any remaining iterations.

questions.question: What does the continue statement do when executed inside a loop?
options: Skips the rest of the current iteration and immediately jumps to the next cycle of the loop
Stops the program permanently
Prints the current line number
Reverses the loop direction
questions.correctAnswer: Skips the rest of the current iteration and immediately jumps to the next cycle of the loop
questions.explanation: continue halts execution of the current iteration and jumps directly to evaluating the next loop iteration.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the pass statement in Python?
options: A null placeholder statement that does nothing, used syntactically where code is required but you have not written logic yet
A password verification function
Passes variables to another computer over the internet
Skips the entire file
questions.correctAnswer: A null placeholder statement that does nothing, used syntactically where code is required but you have not written logic yet
questions.explanation: pass is a syntactic no-op placeholder. It prevents IndentationErrors in empty functions, loops, or classes during development.

questions.question: What sequence does range(0, 10, 2) generate?
options: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 (stepping by 2)
questions.correctAnswer: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8 (stepping by 2)
questions.explanation: The third parameter in range(start, stop, step) defines the step increment: 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.

questions.question: What does the built-in enumerate() function provide when iterating over a collection in a for loop?
options: Both the index number (0, 1, 2...) and the item value simultaneously: for index, item in enumerate(items):
Only odd numbers
The memory address of each variable
A random shuffle of the list
questions.correctAnswer: Both the index number (0, 1, 2...) and the item value simultaneously: for index, item in enumerate(items):
questions.explanation: enumerate(sequence) yields (index, item) pairs, eliminating the need to manually track loop counter variables.

questions.question: Can a while loop in Python have an optional else clause?
options: Yes! The else block executes when the loop condition becomes False naturally, but does NOT run if the loop was exited via break
No, else can only be paired with if statements
Only in Python 2
Yes, but it causes a 5-second delay
questions.correctAnswer: Yes! The else block executes when the loop condition becomes False naturally, but does NOT run if the loop was exited via break
questions.explanation: Python loops support an else block that runs upon natural loop completion without encountering a break.

questions.question: How do you iterate backwards through numbers from 10 down to 1 using range()?
options: range(1, 10).reverse()
range(10 -> 0)
questions.explanation: Passing a negative step (range(10, 0, -1)) counts backwards from 10 down to 1.

questions.question: Which built-in Python data structure is ordered, mutable (changeable), and written with square brackets [ ]?
options: List
Tuple
Set
Dictionary
questions.correctAnswer: List
questions.explanation: Lists are mutable ordered sequences created with square brackets (e.g. items = [1, 2, 3]).

questions.question: How do you add a new single element to the very end of an existing Python list?
options: list_name.append(item)
list_name.push(item)
list_name.add(item)
list_name.insert_end(item)
questions.correctAnswer: list_name.append(item)
questions.explanation: In Python, the append() method adds an item to the end of a list in-place.

questions.question: What is the difference between a List and a Tuple in Python?
options: Lists are mutable (can be modified after creation), whereas Tuples are immutable (cannot be changed after creation)
Tuples can only store numbers
Lists can only store strings
Tuples run in a separate thread
questions.correctAnswer: Lists are mutable (can be modified after creation), whereas Tuples are immutable (cannot be changed after creation)
questions.explanation: Tuples (written with parentheses (1, 2)) are immutable. Once created, items cannot be added, removed, or changed.

questions.question: Which Python data structure stores data as unique, unordered key-value pairs written with curly braces { key: value }?
options: Dictionary (dict)
Array
Tuple
Set
questions.correctAnswer: Dictionary (dict)
questions.explanation: Dictionaries store mappings between unique keys and corresponding values (e.g. {"name": "Ada", "age": 25}).

questions.question: What does a Python Set ({1, 2, 3}) automatically do if you attempt to add duplicate elements?
options: It ignores duplicate values, maintaining only unique elements
It raises a DuplicateError exception
It converts duplicates into negative numbers
It replaces all items with None
questions.correctAnswer: It ignores duplicate values, maintaining only unique elements
questions.explanation: Sets enforce uniqueness. Adding an existing element has no effect, making sets ideal for deduplication and membership testing.

questions.question: What does the slice expression numbers[1:4] return from the list numbers = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]?
options: [20, 30, 40] (from index 1 up to but excluding index 4)
questions.correctAnswer: [20, 30, 40] (from index 1 up to but excluding index 4)
questions.explanation: List slicing [start:stop] extracts items starting at index 1 up to index 3 (20, 30, 40).

questions.question: What is a "List Comprehension" in Python?
options: A concise, readable syntax for creating a new list by transforming or filtering elements from an existing sequence (e.g. [x * 2 for x in nums])
A tool that explains what a list is in plain English
A function that sorts a list alphabetically
A compression algorithm like GZIP
questions.correctAnswer: A concise, readable syntax for creating a new list by transforming or filtering elements from an existing sequence (e.g. [x * 2 for x in nums])
questions.explanation: List comprehensions provide a clean, one-line syntax for mapping and filtering sequences into new lists.

questions.question: How do you safely retrieve a value from a dictionary without crashing if the key does not exist?
options: student.get("grade", "Not Found")
student["grade"]
student.find("grade")
student.readKey("grade")
questions.correctAnswer: student.get("grade", "Not Found")
questions.explanation: dict.get(key, default) safely retrieves a value. If the key is missing, it returns the fallback default instead of raising a KeyError.

questions.question: What is the time complexity of checking if an item exists in a Python Set (item in my_set) compared to a List (item in my_list)?
options: Set lookup is O(1) instantaneous hash lookup, while List lookup is O(N) linear search
List is 10 times faster than Set
Both are exactly the same speed
Sets cannot be searched
questions.correctAnswer: Set lookup is O(1) instantaneous hash lookup, while List lookup is O(N) linear search
questions.explanation: Sets use hash tables under the hood, allowing instant O(1) membership checks regardless of collection size.

questions.question: How do you remove and return the last item from a list in Python?
options: my_list.pop()
my_list.remove_last()
my_list.delete()
my_list.shift()
questions.correctAnswer: my_list.pop()
questions.explanation: pop() removes and returns the element at the given index (defaulting to the last item).

function
fn
func

questions.question: What happens if a Python function finishes executing without an explicit return statement?

It returns 0
It raises an EmptyFunctionError exception
It loops back to the start of the function
questions.correctAnswer: It automatically returns None

def greet(name: default "Student"):
def greet(name := "Student"):
def greet(name or "Student"):
questions.correctAnswer: def greet(name="Student"):
